access.anon: When accessing the authorization page, will first be guided to sign in.
access.user: Can only approve or reject third-party client authorization requests.
access.admin: Can manage OAuth clients in the admin backend.
access.agent: Accesses restricted capabilities after obtaining a token through the standard authorization flow.

rules.auth-page-clarity: The authorization page must clearly display the application name, requested permissions, client-id host when URL-based, redirect host, per-scope controls, approve action, and reject action. Loopback redirects warn that the callback returns to a local application.
rules.user-consent-framing: Users see 'what this app wants and whether I allow it', not protocol details. Users may approve a subset of requested scopes, and the allow action cannot grant scopes outside the signed authorize request. Stored consent binds scopes, resources, and supported UserInfo claims. Consent state accepts Better Auth 1.7 canonical ba_param signatures plus legacy no-ba_param signatures during rollout, validates the declared signed-name set, and strips signing metadata before delegation.
rules.dcr-via-provider: Dynamic client registration remains enabled as a compatibility fallback on the standard /oauth2/register path owned by the upstream @better-auth/mcp plugin, which wraps the Better Auth OAuth provider and returns HTTP 201 Created; the project does not maintain parallel hand-written DCR persistence. Registrations that require DPoP-bound tokens are rejected because the exposed resource servers are Bearer-only.
rules.dcr-device-only-no-redirect: Dynamic client registration for a device-only client may omit redirect_uris; any provider-adapter placeholder redirect URI must not be persisted or returned as registered client metadata.
rules.publication-crawler-client: The publication crawler uses the migration-provisioned public native client life-ustc-publication-crawler. It has no client secret or redirect URI, is limited to the custom device_code plus refresh_token grants and publication.ingest:write plus offline_access scopes, and is never issued through public dynamic client registration. Ingestion still checks that the approving token subject is an administrator.
rules.dcr-rules-from-provider: Provider configuration owns DCR defaults, allowed scopes, client restrictions, PKCE, resources, and zero-second refresh-token reuse. Public DCR advertises only public scopes; admin scopes require admin-created clients. publication.ingest:write is an admin-only REST scope in the full provider vocabulary, excluded from public discovery, DCR, and MCP; every ingestion use-case checks isAdmin. Only canonical feature:action scopes are accepted; REST resource servers enforce audience, active grants, and scopes.
rules.llm-platform-oauth-compatibility: Remote MCP clients use discovery, CIMD, authorization code + PKCE, /api/mcp resource indicators, and protected-resource metadata; DCR remains a fallback. CIMD requires HTTPS URL IDs with exact client_id, non-empty client_name, and redirect_uris. Fetches fail closed unless all A/AAAA answers are public; upstream limits timeout, size, and redirects, while Workers enforce global_fetch_strictly_public. Unsupported grants are filtered; DPoP-only metadata is rejected.
rules.trusted-clients-admin-backend: First-party / internal applications prefer using trusted OAuth clients created in the admin backend; such clients can skip consent and can further be incorporated into the Better Auth provider's trusted / cached client scheme when needed, rather than relying on public DCR.
rules.public-clients-pkce: Public MCP / CLI / native clients use public + PKCE mode and token_endpoint_auth_method=none stores or returns no client secret; the admin inventory must explicitly label trust and fixed authentication type to reduce misconfiguration probability.
rules.user-delegated-grants-only: OAuth discovery metadata advertises only user-delegated grants: authorization_code, refresh_token, and the custom device_code grant. It must not advertise client_credentials unless a real service-account authority model is introduced.
rules.client-validation-from-provider: When creating clients in the admin backend, redirect URI and client metadata validation should reuse Better Auth provider rules rather than a local fork. The 1.7 migration backfills account issuers and keys linked accounts by issuer plus provider subject; a nondefault AUTH_OIDC_ISSUER requires deployment-time reconciliation.
rules.loopback-redirect-tolerance: For public native clients with loopback redirect URIs, the server should accommodate the hostname alias difference between 127.0.0.1 and localhost to avoid DCR registration and authorization requests failing solely due to these two local loopback representations; beyond this, strict matching is maintained for path, query, scheme, and non-loopback host rules.
rules.rest-resource-origin-alias: For compatibility with older CLI and Bot clients, a REST OAuth resource indicator equal to the public site origin may be normalized to the canonical REST issuer resource at /api/auth during authorization, token, device authorization, and refresh-resource validation. The server should still mint and persist tokens against the canonical /api/auth audience, not the bare origin.
rules.device-grant-custom: The device authorization flow remains custom because @better-auth/oauth-provider 1.7.0-rc.2 does not yet export the upstream device grant used by later documentation. It is limited to enabled public clients registered with device_code, and approved resource parameters mint provider-compatible JWT access tokens for REST/MCP audiences. DPoP-bound clients and DPoP proofs fail closed because this custom grant does not verify RFC 9449 proofs.
rules.rest-bearer-scopes: Protected REST and GraphQL endpoints accept OAuth bearer tokens only with the endpoint audience and explicit feature:action authority; shared verification rejects any DPoP-bound cnf.jkt token presented as Bearer. Browser cookie sessions continue to use normal signed-in user semantics without OAuth scopes.
rules.mcp-refresh-resource-binding: Omitted-resource refresh-token requests map to MCP only when the stored grant includes an MCP feature scope and canonical MCP approval. Explicit-resource replacement verifies the current upstream JWT, requires cnf.jkt and token_type to agree, permits a valid Bearer-to-DPoP refresh upgrade, and rejects malformed or conflicting old/current confirmation data instead of downgrading sender constraint.
rules.token-endpoint-observability: OAuth token handling exports whole-request and fixed-stage durations to separate provider, grant validation, request preparation, and response checks. Better Auth solely owns idempotent resource initialization; the token route does not repeat it. Configured resource policies use the provider's write-invalidated cache, never an application token cache. Telemetry never includes token values, authorization codes, refresh tokens, client secrets, cookies, raw errors, or resource values.
rules.oauth-proxy-for-dev: Local development and preview deployments without fixed hostnames can reuse the production site's registered provider callback address through an OAuth proxy; after sharing the proxy encryption key, production completes the callback and returns the encrypted profile to the current instance. Better Auth 1.7 uses /api/auth/callback/{provider-id}; provider redirect allowlists must include it before deployment.
rules.canonical-discovery-paths: Path-bearing issuers and resources expose metadata at canonical path-aware locations: authorization server metadata at /.well-known/oauth-authorization-server/api/auth, OIDC discovery at /api/auth/.well-known/openid-configuration (plus its RFC 8414 path), and MCP protected-resource metadata at /.well-known/oauth-protected-resource/api/mcp. Root-level entries are compatibility redirects; canonical MCP metadata supports GET and bodyless HEAD.
rules.protected-resource-scope-advertisement: Canonical MCP protected-resource metadata is produced by the upstream @better-auth/mcp plugin and exposed through the local path-aware CORS facade. The facade advertises only canonical public non-admin feature:action scopes and removes DPoP metadata because the MCP transport remains Bearer-only. account.client-activity is an explicit read-only feature and no :write scope is generated, registered, or advertised.
rules.mcp-discovery-compatibility-aliases: Because some MCP clients probe resource-relative or issuer-style well-known paths before settling on canonical metadata, /api/mcp/.well-known/oauth-authorization-server, /.well-known/oauth-authorization-server/api/mcp, /api/mcp/.well-known/openid-configuration, and /.well-known/openid-configuration/api/mcp should redirect to the issuer metadata used by the MCP protected resource.
rules.discovery-alias-routing: Compatibility aliases redirect to canonical metadata instead of returning inconsistent JSON. A shared route-target table keeps canonical responses and alias redirects aligned as paths change.
rules.discovery-cors: Discovery metadata should support cross-origin reading; at minimum return Access-Control-Allow-Origin: * for OpenID discovery, and keep the CORS behavior of authorization server metadata and protected resource metadata consistent, reducing compatibility risks for browser-type clients and debugging tools.
rules.transport-cors: The MCP transport endpoint /api/mcp should also support browser-based clients and debugging tools using Bearer tokens: answer OPTIONS preflights, allow the MCP-specific request headers, and expose MCP-Session-Id and WWW-Authenticate on cross-origin transport responses.
rules.transport-origin-validation: Per the MCP Streamable HTTP transport guidance, /api/mcp should reject requests carrying an Origin header unless that origin matches the app's trusted origin set (public/canonical origin, localhost dev aliases, and allowed preview hosts). Non-browser clients that omit Origin remain supported.

rules.oauth-usage-aggregation: Successful and failed completed OAuth operations are coalesced within a Worker into bounded per-grant, Shanghai-day, feature, and channel counters before atomic upsert. Rows contain no request targets, arguments, content, network, device, token, or secret data. The authorization page sums the current grant's last 30 days and selects the latest feature/channel by lastUsedAt.
rules.recent-auth-for-consent: Approving a new grant or extending an existing authorization requires an authoritative server-side session created within the last 15 minutes. A stale attempt records a denied audit event and returns explicit sign-out/sign-in guidance without issuing a code.
rules.ownership-scoped-transaction: Revocation requires an authoritative server-side session created within the last 15 minutes, then transactionally removes every consent, access-token row, refresh-token row, approved or pending device-code row, and usage aggregate for the signed-in user and client together with its audit event.
rules.active-user-grant-enforcement: User JWTs, opaque access tokens, and refresh tokens bind the exact consent generation and scopes that issued them. REST, GraphQL, MCP, userinfo, and introspection require that generation to remain active; reauthorization cannot revive old tokens and scope reduction cannot retain broader access. Admin-created skipConsent clients are the only bypass and still require an existing user. Missing evidence and database errors fail closed. Lookups stay uncached so revocation applies on the next request.
rules.refresh-revocation-race: Refresh exchange verifies the hashed token row and exact grant generation before delegation, preserves that generation on the returned JWT, opaque access token, and rotated refresh token, then verifies it again before returning success. If revocation or reauthorization wins the race, only the old lineage rows are purged and no token can continue under the newer grant.
rules.singleton-form-parameters: OAuth token and introspection form parameters are single-valued and repeated values fail with invalid_request before delegation; resource remains multi-valued.
rules.consent-mutations: The provider update-consent and delete-consent routes are intercepted and reimplemented with ownership checks, trusted-origin enforcement, token cleanup, and grant-generation rotation. Direct provider consent mutation is unavailable; the authorization page is the only consent entry point.

device-authorization-grant.title: Device Authorization Grant (RFC 8628)
device-authorization-grant.description: No MCP tool starts device authorization; bearer tokens minted by this flow can call REST and MCP when the approved device request is resource-bound and scoped appropriately, including feature:read/feature:write for REST.

routes.returns: { device_code, user_code, verification_uri, verification_uri_complete, expires_in, interval }
notes: The client must be an enabled public client registered with urn:ietf:params:oauth:grant-type:device_code; omitted scope defaults to low-risk openid/profile scopes allowed by the client, while optional repeated resource parameters are validated against provider audiences and persisted with the pending device code.
Supports CORS (Access-Control-Allow-Origin: *); OPTIONS returns a 204 CORS preflight response.
.well-known/openid-configuration already includes device_authorization_endpoint and urn:ietf:params:oauth:grant-type:device_code in grant_types_supported.
Supports unauthenticated browser preflight for public OAuth device authorization clients.

routes.returns: { access_token, token_type, expires_in, expires_at?, refresh_token?, scope?, id_token? } | { error, error_description? }
notes: The device polls this endpoint with grant_type=urn:ietf:params:oauth:grant-type:device_code and device_code to obtain an access token.

If resource parameters are included while polling, they must match the resources approved through the device authorization request; resource-bound device grants return JWT access tokens accepted by matching REST/MCP audiences, but protected REST routes still require matching feature:read/feature:write scopes.
A refresh token is returned only for resource-less device grants when the approved scope includes offline_access; resource-bound device grants do not issue refresh tokens.
During polling, returns authorization_pending, slow_down, expired_token, access_denied, invalid_scope, or invalid_grant error codes based on state.

fields: One segmented user-code input labelled Device Code
